prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, a general catalytic method for constructing aryl amines

statement.case_for: After the full first round I still prefer B051, and I want to say why in terms of what is new chemically. Before Buchwald and Hartwig, Kosugi's 1983 coupling of aryl bromides with tin amides was a stoichiometric-in-tin reaction of narrow scope that needed a preformed, toxic aminostannane. The step that made aryl amination a general method was the 1995-96 move to a catalytic reaction using free amines and a base, which required new ligand logic: chelating and then bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines that suppress beta-hydride elimination from the palladium amide and speed C-N reductive elimination, followed by the ligand generations that extended the reaction to primary amines, amides, heteroarenes and aryl chlorides. Buchwald and Hartwig developed these in parallel and each carried the mechanistic work through, so the credit is two names and not a negotiated trio. The result is checkable: this is among the most used reactions in medicinal chemistry and process routes, and it replaced harsh nucleophilic aromatic substitution and Ullmann-type conditions. Maturity is not in question, the principle is simple, and a citation can state it in one sentence.
statement.case_against: The 2010 palladium cross-coupling prize is the obvious objection. I do not think it bars this prize, because the C-N problem needed its own mechanistic solution, but I accept that several colleagues will read it as a sequel to an honoured idea. B051 also generates less new science than B056: it is a superb general method and not a new class of targets or a new modality. Kosugi's precedent is a real piece of history that the citation wording has to respect. Finally, B056 has a much broader base of support in this committee (seven of eight members put it in their preferred configuration, four of them first at the opening) and I am the only member whose preferred ballot is outside it, so I should show that my position rests on chemistry and not on stubbornness.

responses.point: Linke asks whether the original C-N discovery can be separated from Kosugi's precedent and from the 2010 prize closely enough to support a stand-alone citation, and says he can separate degraders more cleanly.
responses.response: Against Kosugi: his reaction used an isolated tin amide, was limited to a few secondary amines, and had no route to a catalytic reaction on the free amine. The 1995 Buchwald in situ tin amide work and the 1995-96 tin-free reactions of Hartwig and Buchwald with alkoxide bases changed what the reaction was, namely a catalytic coupling of an amine with an aryl halide that depends on ligand design. Against 2010: the Heck, Negishi and Suzuki couplings share a transmetalation step with a carbon nucleophile, whereas C-N coupling has no organometallic partner and its limiting steps (amido formation, suppression of beta-hydride elimination, C-N reductive elimination) are different. I grant that your generative-potential criterion favours B056 and I will not claim otherwise. My point is that B051 passes a different criterion, namely a general method with verified adoption, and the citation can be written without a priority dispute.

responses.point: Zou asks for the argument that C-N coupling is a distinct principle and not a refinement of the 2010 prize, since a second prize needs that justification.
responses.response: The argument is mechanistic. In C-C coupling, reductive elimination from a palladium organometallic intermediate is easy and the difficult step is usually making the partners meet. For nitrogen, the palladium amide is prone to beta-hydride elimination and reductive elimination of the C-N bond is hard, so the early reactions failed for most amines. The solution was ligands, not a new partner. That is why it took about fifteen years after the first cross-couplings, and why the success is attributable to identifiable ligand innovations by two groups. I think this is as distinct from 2010 as the Suzuki reaction is from the Heck reaction, though I understand that a committee that wants a strictly new principle may still decline it.

responses.point: Aqvist moved his third B056 seat to Handa, and he says he could see B051 as a second part if the committee wanted a mature synthetic method.
responses.response: A two-part prize of B056 and B051 would need more than three names in total, since Crews and Deshaies already fill two seats and Buchwald and Hartwig would add two. I do not think the committee should shorten either credit to fit. If B056 is the prize, I would rather the committee decide it entirely on its own merits than add a method part for balance.

responses.point: Aili argues for Crews, Deshaies and Handa under one citation about recruiting E3 ligases, and would not split PROTACs and glues unless no unified wording can be found.
responses.response: Answering the chair's question on the third seat: if B056 proceeds, I find Handa's case more chemically concrete than Ciulli's. The cereblon identification is a datable mechanistic discovery that explains thalidomide and underlies most clinical glue and PROTAC chemistry, whereas the VHL ligand work, valuable as it is, is ligand and linker optimization of the kind I described in round 1. Aili's point that one citation can cover both strands is credible if it is worded around recruitment of ubiquitin ligases and not around bifunctional molecules. I still would not call the absence of an approved degrader fatal, since the principle has been reproduced widely, but I do give B056 less weight than B051 on maturity of impact.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the 2010 cross-coupling prize as a real obstacle; this decides B051 for most members and is a judgment, not a fact I can resolve.
The exact weight of Kosugi's precedent and of the 1995-96 priority sequence, which I recall from the literature and have not re-verified.
Whether the third seat in B056 should be Handa or Ciulli, and how the expert report divides the VHL and ternary-complex framework from the Crews laboratory.
Whether no approved degrader to date makes B056 early; I am relying on recollection of trial status.
Whether a two-person prize for Buchwald and Hartwig is too narrow given the breadth of their other work.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no mentoring, institutional or collaborative tie to Buchwald, Hartwig, Kosugi or any credited name on B056 or B017. My Masamune lineage does not touch these areas. I sit on the committee with fellow Lund professors Linke and Sparr, which is a collegial connection with no bearing on any shortlisted candidate.
